question: Can I claim registered massage therapy as a medical expense on my Canadian tax return?
reference_answer: Only when the massage therapist is a medical practitioner authorized to practise under the laws of the province or territory where the service is provided. You can claim only the part your health plan did not reimburse.

question: Which 12-month period can I use when claiming medical expenses on my tax return?
reference_answer: You can claim eligible expenses paid in any 12-month period ending in the tax year that you did not claim in a previous year (a 24-month period including the date of death applies for a person who died).

question: My insurance reimbursed most of my prescription glasses. Can I claim the rest as a medical expense?
reference_answer: Yes. Eyeglasses or contact lenses prescribed by an optometrist or medical doctor are eligible, and you can claim the portion you paid that was not reimbursed.

question: What is the difference between line 33099 and line 33199?
reference_answer: Line 33099 is for expenses for yourself, your spouse or common-law partner, and your dependent children under 18. Line 33199 is for expenses for other dependants, such as adult children or other relatives who depended on you.

question: Can the premiums I pay for my extended health plan count as a medical expense?
reference_answer: Yes. Premiums you paid to a private health services plan can be claimed, but not amounts paid by your employer or amounts that were reimbursed.

question: Is a gym membership an eligible medical expense for the Canadian tax credit?
reference_answer: No. Fees for athletic or fitness clubs are listed among expenses that are not eligible medical expenses.

question: Can I claim travel costs when I have to travel to get medical care that isn't available near home?
reference_answer: If equivalent care is not available near home you may claim transportation costs when you travel at least 40 km, and other reasonable travel expenses such as meals and accommodation when you travel at least 80 km, subject to the conditions in the guide.

question: What is the Public Service Health Care Plan?
reference_answer: It is the private health care plan for federal public service employees, pensioners and their eligible dependants, which reimburses eligible expenses not covered by provincial or territorial health insurance.

question: Does the Public Service Health Care Plan replace provincial health insurance?
reference_answer: No. The plan supplements provincial or territorial health insurance; it pays for eligible services and supplies that the public plan does not cover.

question: Who can qualify for the Canadian Dental Care Plan?
reference_answer: Canadian residents for tax purposes who do not have access to dental insurance, have an adjusted family net income under the plan's limit ($90,000) and have filed their tax return can qualify.

question: Will the Canadian Dental Care Plan pay the full cost of my dental treatment?
reference_answer: Not always. The plan covers a defined set of services, some need preauthorization, a co-payment may apply depending on family income, and a provider may charge extra fees that the plan does not cover.

question: What are the principles of the Canada Health Act?
reference_answer: Public administration, comprehensiveness, universality, portability and accessibility.

question: Does the Canada Health Act allow extra-billing or user charges for insured services?
reference_answer: No. Extra-billing and user charges for insured health services are discouraged through mandatory deductions from federal cash transfers to the province or territory.

question: Does OHIP pay for prescription eyeglasses for adults in Ontario?
reference_answer: No. OHIP covers some eye examinations for eligible people (for example children and seniors, or people with certain medical conditions) but it does not pay for glasses or contact lenses.

question: What do I need to bring to apply for an Ontario health card?
reference_answer: You apply in person at ServiceOntario with original documents that prove your citizenship or immigration status, your Ontario residency and your identity.

question: What is the maximum waiting period for pre-existing conditions on Australian hospital cover?
reference_answer: 12 months, except for hospital psychiatric services, rehabilitation and palliative care, where the maximum is 2 months.

question: How long is the waiting period for pregnancy and birth on hospital cover?
reference_answer: Insurers can apply a waiting period of up to 12 months for pregnancy and birth.

question: Do I have to serve my waiting periods again if I switch health insurers?
reference_answer: Not for benefits you have already served waiting periods for, if you switch to an equivalent or lower level of cover; you may have to serve waiting periods for any higher or new benefits.

question: What are the hospital product tiers in Australia?
reference_answer: Gold, Silver, Bronze and Basic, each with minimum clinical categories that must be covered; insurers can also offer Plus versions of Silver, Bronze and Basic.

question: What does the Plus in Silver Plus mean?
reference_answer: A Plus policy covers the minimum clinical categories for its tier plus some additional categories from a higher tier.

question: What does a Gold hospital policy have to cover?
reference_answer: A Gold policy must cover all of the hospital clinical categories.

question: What does restricted cover mean for a hospital clinical category?
reference_answer: Restricted cover pays benefits similar to treatment as a private patient in a public hospital; if you go to a private hospital for that treatment you are likely to face large out-of-pocket costs.

question: What is the Lifetime Health Cover loading?
reference_answer: A loading of 2% on hospital cover premiums for every year you are over 30 when you first take out hospital cover after your Lifetime Health Cover base day, up to a maximum of 70%.

question: Does the Lifetime Health Cover loading ever stop?
reference_answer: Yes. The loading is removed after you have held hospital cover continuously for 10 years.

question: What is the Medicare Levy Surcharge?
reference_answer: An extra levy of 1% to 1.5% of income for Australian taxpayers above the income threshold who do not hold an appropriate level of private hospital cover.

question: Will extras-only cover stop me paying the Medicare Levy Surcharge?
reference_answer: No. To avoid the surcharge you need an appropriate level of private hospital cover; extras (general treatment) cover alone does not count.

question: How does the Australian Government Rebate on private health insurance work?
reference_answer: The government contributes an income-tested percentage of your premium, which you can take as a premium reduction or claim through your tax return; the rebate percentages are adjusted each year on 1 April.

question: What does Medicare cover if I am treated in a public hospital?
reference_answer: As a public patient in a public hospital, Medicare covers your treatment and accommodation at no cost, but you generally cannot choose your doctor.

question: Why can I still have out-of-pocket costs in a private hospital when I have hospital cover?
reference_answer: Doctors can charge more than the Medicare Benefits Schedule fee and the amount covered by your insurer's gap arrangements, and you may also pay an excess or co-payment or for items your policy does not cover.

question: Does Medicare pay for dental check-ups and glasses?
reference_answer: Generally no. Most dental and optical services are not covered by Medicare; extras (general treatment) cover from a private insurer can pay benefits for them.
